basic_identification.name: Commons vs. enclosure in digital art
basic_identification.originator: Theoretical: Lawrence Lessig (Creative Commons, Free Culture), James Boyle (enclosure of the digital commons), Elinor Ostrom (commons governance). Open Future foundation (2024 report on digital commons as public infrastructure). Tools: Creative Commons (founded 2001), GNU/copyleft movement, Blender Foundation, Processing Foundation. Art context: open-source generative art tools, CC-licensed art, Art Blocks Engine (open infrastructure), versus proprietary platforms (Adobe, OpenSea, Instagram). Sciences Po research on CC and property rights conflict.
basic_identification.geography: Global discourse. Creative Commons (US-founded, globally adopted). European digital commons policy (EU Digital Decade). Open-source communities globally distributed.

core_ideas.core_claim: Digital art exists in a structural tension between commons (shared tools, open licenses, public infrastructure, collective knowledge) and enclosure (proprietary platforms, all-rights-reserved IP, walled gardens, vendor lock-in). Post-NFT-crash, the field is at an inflection point: will surviving infrastructure trend toward commons (open standards, shared vocabularies, portable identity) or enclosure (platform lock-in, proprietary AI models, closed data)? The 2024 Open Future report identifies digital commons as a key mechanism for providing public digital infrastructure, offering an alternative to enclosure strategies of governments and major digital service providers.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Digital art is uniquely positioned in this tension because the medium is inherently copyable (digital files reproduce perfectly), yet markets depend on artificial scarcity (NFTs, DRM, platform exclusivity). Open-source tools (Blender, Krita, Processing, p5.js) enable art creation without proprietary dependencies. However, distribution and discovery remain enclosed by platform monopolies. The commons/enclosure tension is more acute in digital art than physical art because the cost of sharing is near-zero while the incentive to enclose is driven by platform business models.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The attention economy is an enclosure mechanism: platforms enclose audience attention and ration access through algorithms. Open commons (personal websites, RSS feeds, federated social media) provide attention-independent distribution but lack discovery scale. The tension: artists can create with open tools but must distribute through enclosed platforms. Attention economy platforms benefit from the commons (open-source code, free content) while enclosing the value generated.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Commons infrastructure serves intention (shared tools, transparent standards, collective knowledge serve the declared needs of the field). Enclosure serves capture (platform lock-in, proprietary data, artificial scarcity serve extraction). The field's structural health depends on the balance between these forces. Post-crash, there is an opportunity for intention-native commons infrastructure, but the economic incentives still favor enclosure.

market_economics.revenue_model: Commons: grant-funded (Processing Foundation, Blender Foundation), donation-supported (Creative Commons), community-maintained (open-source projects), institutional (museum open-access programs). Enclosure: subscription (Adobe Creative Cloud ~$55/month), platform fees (OpenSea 2.5%, Foundation 5%), data monetization (social media platforms), proprietary licensing. Hybrid: some tools are open-source but offer paid services (Blender with commercial add-ons). The MIT/permissive license risk: open-source code taken into proprietary software without reciprocal contribution.
market_economics.market_position: Commons and enclosure operate across all levels of the value chain. Creation tools: Blender/Krita (commons) vs. Adobe (enclosure). Distribution: personal websites (commons) vs. Instagram/OpenSea (enclosure). Discovery: word-of-mouth/curation (commons) vs. algorithmic recommendation (enclosure). Preservation: IPFS/Arweave (commons) vs. platform-dependent storage (enclosure). The field's infrastructure is a patchwork of commons and enclosed layers.
market_economics.price_range: Commons tools are free or donation-based. Enclosed tools range from $10-55+/month subscription. CC-licensed art is free to use under license terms. All-rights-reserved digital art priced by market. The price differential between commons and enclosed tools creates access inequality: free tools democratize creation, enclosed platforms gate distribution.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Open-source art tools growing steadily: Blender user base expanding, Krita active development, p5.js web editor adoption increasing. Proprietary tools (Adobe) maintaining dominance but facing pressure from open alternatives and AI integration. Creative Commons adoption stable but not growing dramatically. Platform enclosure intensifying through AI integration (Meta AI, algorithmic opacity). The trend is paradoxical: open tools growing while enclosed platforms deepening lock-in. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: Commons-oriented collectors: institutional (museums acquiring CC-licensed works), academic (research use under fair use/CC), and community-oriented collectors valuing open culture. Enclosure-oriented collectors: investment-focused (valuing scarcity and exclusivity), platform-native (collecting within specific marketplace ecosystems). The demographics map roughly onto commons (public, institutional, academic) vs. enclosure (private, commercial, speculative). [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: Commons infrastructure depends on grants, donations, and volunteer labor - sustainable but chronically underfunded. Enclosure infrastructure is commercially sustainable but extracts value from creative labor. Copyleft (GPL, CC-SA) provides legal sustainability for commons by requiring derivative works to remain open. The long-term sustainability question: can commons infrastructure compete with commercially-funded enclosure without adequate public investment? The Open Future report argues for public funding of digital commons as infrastructure.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Commons: Blender (3D), Krita (2D painting), GIMP (image editing), Inkscape (vector), Processing/p5.js (creative coding), Audacity (audio), OpenFrameworks, Arduino/Raspberry Pi (hardware), LibreOffice. Enclosure: Adobe Creative Suite (Photoshop, Illustrator, After Effects, Premiere), Autodesk (Maya, 3ds Max), Procreate (iPad), proprietary DAWs. Hybrid: TouchDesigner (proprietary but widely used in generative art), Unity/Unreal (proprietary with free tiers).
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI intensifies the commons/enclosure tension. Open-source AI models (Stable Diffusion, Llama) enable commons-based AI art creation. Proprietary AI (DALL-E, Midjourney) enclose capabilities behind subscriptions and API fees. AI training data debate is fundamentally a commons/enclosure conflict: do creative works in the commons (internet, libraries) constitute a training data commons, or does their use for AI training represent enclosure of creative labor? The EU AI Act's copyright provisions and opt-out mechanisms attempt to navigate this tension.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Commons tools enable diverse liveness: Processing for real-time generative art, Blender for animation, Arduino for interactive installations. Enclosure can limit liveness through DRM, platform-specific formats, and subscription dependency (if subscription lapses, tools become unavailable). The liveness of art practice depends on tool accessibility, which commons ensure more durably than enclosed alternatives.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Open source, proprietary, Creative Commons, copyleft, public domain, walled garden, vendor lock-in, digital commons, digital enclosure, platform capitalism, data sovereignty, interoperability, forking, permissive vs. copyleft licensing, free culture, free software. The vocabulary combines legal (licensing), political (commons/enclosure), economic (platform capitalism), and technical (interoperability) registers. It is adequate for structural analysis but underused in art criticism.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: This discourse explicitly maps the tension between openness and enclosure, commons and capture. Open-source tools and CC licensing are maximally open and commons-oriented. Proprietary platforms and all-rights-reserved IP are maximally enclosed and capture-oriented. The field occupies the full spectrum. Infrastructure tendency: commons tools build infrastructure. Enclosure tends toward spectacle (platform-optimized content). Collective vs individual: commons inherently collective, enclosure often individual-focused.

infrastructure_governance.openness: The full spectrum. Fully open: GPL/copyleft software (Blender, Krita), CC-licensed art, public domain works. Fully enclosed: proprietary software (Adobe DRM), platform-locked content, all-rights-reserved with active enforcement. The critical middle ground: MIT/permissive licensed code that can be taken into proprietary products (the enclosure of commons resources). Copyleft provides stronger protection against enclosure than permissive licenses.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Commons: community governance (Blender Foundation, Processing Foundation), non-profit boards, contributor communities. Enclosure: corporate governance (Adobe, Meta, OpenSea). Creative Commons: non-profit with board of directors. Open-source governance varies: benevolent dictator (Blender's Ton Roosendaal), meritocratic committees, democratic processes. The governance question: who decides the rules of the commons, and can they prevent enclosure?
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Commons: open data, exportable, user-controlled. CC-licensed works are reusable under license terms. Open-source tools process data locally. Enclosure: platform-controlled data, limited export, user-generated content licensed to platform. The sovereignty gap: artists can create with sovereign tools (open-source) but must surrender sovereignty when distributing through enclosed platforms.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Commons tools generally support open standards: SVG, OBJ, glTF, JSON, standard code languages. Enclosure creates proprietary formats: PSD, AI, proprietary blockchain token standards. Interoperability is a commons value; incompatibility is an enclosure strategy. The field's interoperability depends on which layer (creation, distribution, discovery, preservation) is examined.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Commons: open formats ensure long-term readability. Source code in open languages (JavaScript, Python) is preservable. CC-licensed works can be archived freely. Enclosure: proprietary formats may become unreadable (obsolescence risk). Platform-dependent storage at risk of closure. DRM prevents archiving. The commons provides structurally superior preservation because it does not depend on any single entity's continued operation.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Creative Commons licenses are explicit consent instruments: artists choose CC-BY, CC-BY-SA, CC-BY-NC etc. to specify exactly how their work may be used. This is the most sophisticated consent architecture in digital art. Proprietary platforms use binary consent (accept ToS or don't use service) with no granularity. Copyleft extends consent through time: future users must maintain the same freedom. The commons/enclosure tension is fundamentally about consent: who decides how creative works can be used?

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The traditional art world is primarily enclosure-oriented: gallery exclusivity, all-rights-reserved IP, physical scarcity, restricted access. Museums are partial exceptions (public access mission). The digital art commons offers an alternative model: art can be shared, remixed, and collectively maintained. However, the traditional art market's economic model depends on scarcity and exclusivity, creating tension with commons values. Some traditional institutions are adopting open access (Getty Open Content, Smithsonian Open Access) but these remain exceptional.
field_position.what_it_enables: Commons tools enable: art creation without financial barriers (free software), global collaboration (open-source development), remix culture (CC licensing), collective knowledge building (shared code libraries, tutorials). Enclosure enables: commercial sustainability for tool developers (Adobe), market value through scarcity (NFTs), platform scale (network effects). The tension is productive: commons enable creation, enclosure enables monetization.
field_position.what_it_lacks: A unified strategy for the digital art field. No coordinated effort to build commons infrastructure for art discovery, provenance, or valuation. No digital art equivalent of Wikipedia or OpenStreetMap. No arts-specific public digital infrastructure funded at the level the Open Future report advocates. The commons lacks scale; the enclosure lacks ethics. Neither provides a complete infrastructure for the field.
field_position.who_is_excluded: From commons: artists without technical literacy to use open-source tools (steeper learning curves than commercial software). Artists in educational systems that teach proprietary tools exclusively (Adobe in design schools). From enclosure: artists who cannot afford subscriptions ($660/year for Adobe CC). Artists in regions with limited payment infrastructure. Artists whose practice conflicts with platform terms of service. The commons/enclosure divide maps onto a competence divide (technical literacy) and an economic divide (subscription costs).
field_position.frontier_signal: Established tension with frontier developments. The AI training data debate is the current frontier: is the internet commons a training data commons? EU AI Act opt-out provisions and CC license interpretation for AI training are actively contested frontier issues. Decentralized social media (ActivityPub, Farcaster) represents a frontier attempt to create commons-based distribution infrastructure.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Commons: word of mouth, community forums (Reddit, Hacker News), open-source project repositories (GitHub), CC search engines, institutional recommendations. Enclosure: algorithmic recommendation (Instagram, TikTok), marketplace trending lists (OpenSea), proprietary search (Google). Discovery is currently dominated by enclosed platforms; commons-based discovery is available but lacks scale and ease-of-use.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Commons infrastructure has low attention dependency: open-source tools work regardless of trending status. CC-licensed works are available regardless of social media attention. Enclosure infrastructure has high attention dependency: platform visibility requires algorithmic favor. The commons provides a more durable base but less discovery amplification.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Commons is inherently intention-aligned: shared tools serve the declared needs of the field. Enclosure may serve intention (professional tools enabling high-quality work) or capture (platform lock-in extracting value). The ideal is commons creation tools with intention-aligned discovery - currently unrealized at scale.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: The commons discourse is itself about commons contribution. Creative Commons licenses, open-source tools, and public domain works are the primary commons contributions in digital art. The discourse identifies what prevents greater commons contribution (economic incentives, lock-in effects) and proposes mechanisms for expanding the commons (public funding, copyleft licensing, open standards).

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: The commons/enclosure discourse tracks neither ownership nor meaning provenance directly. Instead, it tracks usage provenance: how works are licensed, who can use them, under what conditions. CC licenses create a specific form of provenance: the license terms accompany the work through all uses. This is a form of intention provenance: recording the creator's declared intentions about how their work should circulate.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical: the commons/enclosure tension has centuries of precedent (English enclosure acts, digital commons debates). Cyclical: periods of commons expansion (early internet, Creative Commons founding) alternate with enclosure (platform consolidation, AI training data capture). The current moment is a potential turning point post-crash, where the field could move in either direction.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The commons discourse explicitly addresses what is absent: public digital infrastructure for the arts, open standards for digital art metadata, shared vocabularies, portable identity. It frames absence as structural (the result of enclosure) rather than natural. The discourse names what should exist but does not, making it one of the most absence-aware discourses in the field.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence without consensus. Multiple valid positions coexist: copyleft maximalism (everything should be free/open), pragmatic licensing (CC-BY-NC for personal protection with sharing), market realism (enclosure is necessary for sustainability), and hybrid approaches. No consensus on the right balance between openness and protection. The discourse accommodates productive disagreement about means while sharing directional values about commons.
coherence.contestability: Highly contestable. Every licensing choice is debatable. The AI training data debate shows active contestation between commons advocates (training on public data is fair use) and rights advocates (training without consent is theft). The MIT vs GPL debate within open source is a decades-long contestation about the right form of openness. The discourse thrives on contestation.
coherence.forkability: Maximally forkable by design. Open-source software is literally forkable. CC-licensed works are explicitly reusable. The commons provides the legal and technical infrastructure for forking. Enclosure restricts forkability through DRM, proprietary formats, and restrictive licenses. The commons/enclosure tension is partly about who has the right to fork.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: CC licensing as a consent model for contributed knowledge. Open standards for data formats and APIs. The commons-first principle: default to sharing unless there is a specific reason to restrict. Copyleft-style provisions that prevent A(DAI) commons data from being enclosed by proprietary platforms. The Open Future model of digital commons as public infrastructure. The insight that preservation is structurally stronger in the commons than in enclosed systems.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The naive assumption that openness alone creates sustainability (commons infrastructure requires funding). The permissive-license trap: MIT-style openness that allows commons resources to be enclosed by commercial actors. Platform-mediated distribution that surrenders data sovereignty. All-rights-reserved defaults that prevent knowledge sharing. The assumption that artists will contribute to commons without receiving value in return.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) is designed as commons-first infrastructure in a field dominated by enclosure. The tension: how to build a commons that is valuable enough to attract participation while remaining open enough to resist enclosure. How to fund commons infrastructure without commercial capture. How to interface with enclosed platforms (Instagram, OpenSea) without being absorbed by them. The structural tension is between A(DAI)'s commons aspiration and the field's enclosure reality.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Creative Commons licenses are internationally recognized but untested in many jurisdictions. EU AI Act copyright provisions directly address the commons/enclosure tension in AI training data. DMCA safe harbors affect platform liability for user-uploaded content. EU Digital Markets Act targets platform gatekeeper behavior (a form of anti-enclosure regulation). Open Future advocates for EU policy supporting digital commons as public infrastructure.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: The full spectrum: public domain (CC0), attribution (CC-BY), share-alike/copyleft (CC-BY-SA), non-commercial (CC-BY-NC), all-rights-reserved (traditional copyright), and copyleft software licenses (GPL, AGPL). The IP model is the primary mechanism for navigating the commons/enclosure tension. Each license choice positions a work on the openness-enclosure axis.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Commons participation is opt-in: artists choose to apply CC licenses. Enclosure is often default: copyright applies automatically, platform terms accepted by default. The EU AI Act introduces an opt-out model for AI training: creative works are available for training unless creators actively opt out. This is a contentious compromise: commons advocates want opt-in to training, while AI developers want opt-out (or no restriction). The opt-in/opt-out framing is central to the current policy debate.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Commons tools have low platform dependency: Blender, Krita, Processing run locally without cloud dependency. CC licenses are platform-independent. However, commons distribution still depends on platforms (GitHub for code, social media for visibility). Enclosure has high platform dependency by design: Adobe Creative Cloud requires internet connection, platform content locked to platform. The ecosystem is characterized by commons creation with enclosed distribution.
ecosystem.network_effects: Commons benefit from network effects differently than enclosure: more users of open-source tools create more tutorials, plugins, and community support. CC-licensed works create a growing commons that benefits all users. Enclosure network effects create lock-in: more users on a platform make leaving harder. The network effects are qualitatively different: commons network effects are additive (more value for everyone), enclosure network effects are extractive (more value for the platform).
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Post-crash, the commons/enclosure balance is shifting. Speculative enclosure (NFT marketplaces) collapsed. Surviving infrastructure includes both commons (open-source tools, CC-licensed works) and enclosure (Adobe, Instagram). The post-crash opportunity: with speculative incentives removed, the field can more clearly evaluate what commons infrastructure it needs. The trajectory is: commons creation tools stable and growing, enclosed platforms consolidating and integrating AI, commons distribution infrastructure still missing.
